title: SQLAlchemy, asyncpg and Alembic: pools and schema migrations
description: SQLAlchemy QueuePool and asyncpg pool settings, connection arithmetic across workers, pre-ping, and Alembic migrations including zero-downtime practices.
source: SQLAlchemy 2.0 documentation (connection pooling, pool_pre_ping); asyncpg documentation (create_pool); Alembic documentation (autogenerate, operations, autocommit_block); PostgreSQL documentation (max_connections, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY)
seriesDescription: ORM, loading strategies and N+1, transactions, raw SQL, pools and Alembic. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: Match each symptom with the most appropriate first response.

left.text: SQLAlchemy: `"QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out"`
psycopg: `"server closed the connection unexpectedly"` after a quiet night
PostgreSQL: `"FATAL: sorry, too many clients already"`

right.text: Return connections sooner: close sessions, shorten transactions, no slow I/O inside them
Enable `pool_pre_ping` or a `pool_recycle` shorter than the server or firewall idle timeout
Cap per-process pool sizes or put PgBouncer in front of the database
Pass a timeout to `acquire()` and release connections promptly with `async with`
Switch the pool to `NullPool` and open a connection per query

questions.explanation: Exhaustion (waiting for a free connection) and stale connections (dead sockets in the pool) look different but both show up as pool errors. Raising `max_connections` only moves the memory cost to the database.

questions.prompt: Create the SQLAlchemy `engine` `engine` for the URL in `DATABASE_URL` with a pool of 10 connections, at most 5 extra overflow connections, a 10 second wait for a free connection, and a liveness check on checkout.
questions.model:
engine = create_engine(
    DATABASE_URL, pool_size=10, max_overflow=5,
    pool_timeout=10, pool_pre_ping=True)
questions.explanation: Defaults of the `QueuePool` are `pool_size=5`, `max_overflow=10`, `pool_timeout=30`. The hard cap per process is `pool_size + max_overflow`; remember to multiply by the number of processes.

questions.prompt: Using asyncpg and a DSN string `dsn`, create a pool with a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 10 connections, then acquire a connection from it and read the number of rows in table `orders` into `n`.

checks.label: acquires a connection with async with pool.acquire()
awaits a query such as fetchval

questions.model:
pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(dsn, min_size=2, max_size=10)
async with pool.acquire() as conn:
    n = await conn.fetchval("SELECT count(*) FROM orders")
questions.explanation: Create the pool once at application start (for example in a FastAPI `lifespan` handler), not per request. asyncpg placeholders are `$1`, `$2`, and the default pool is `min_size=10`, `max_size=10`.

questions.prompt: Each `uvicorn` worker process creates its own SQLAlchemy engine with `pool_size=5` and `max_overflow=5`. A pod runs 4 workers and the service runs 3 pods. At most how many connections can the service hold open against PostgreSQL?
questions.explanation: Each process can reach `pool_size + max_overflow = 10` connections; `3 pods x 4 workers x 10 = 120`. Pools are per process, so the total scales with workers and autoscaling; compare it with `max_connections`.

questions.prompt: An engine uses the default `pool_size=5` and `max_overflow=10`. 20 requests arrive together and each holds a connection for a long time. How many of them must wait for a connection to be returned?
questions.explanation: The pool can hand out at most `5 + 10 = 15` connections at once, so `20 - 15 = 5` requests wait (and fail after `pool_timeout`, 30 s by default, if none is released).

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: With `pool_pre_ping=True` SQLAlchemy tests a pooled connection with a lightweight ping on checkout and replaces it if it is dead.
questions.reason: Pre-ping adds a small extra round trip to every checkout.

whys.a: Wrong: the extra round trip is a cost, not the reason pre-ping works.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is a drawback, not an explanation of how dead connections are detected.

questions.explanation: The small cost is usually worth it behind firewalls or load balancers that silently drop idle connections. `pool_recycle` is the complementary time-based setting.

questions.prompt: True or false: `pool_size=5` is a hard cap on the number of connections a SQLAlchemy `QueuePool` will open.

options.why: Wrong: `max_overflow` allows extra, temporary connections beyond pool_size.
Correct: the cap is `pool_size + max_overflow`; overflow connections are closed when returned.

questions.explanation: Set `max_overflow=0` for a strict cap. Remember that every process has its own pool.

questions.prompt: True or false: `asyncpg.create_pool()` without size arguments creates a pool with `min_size=10` and `max_size=10`.

options.why: Correct: those are asyncpg's defaults, so unset sizes mean ten connections opened up front.
Wrong: the defaults do give a fixed ten-connection pool.

questions.explanation: Create the pool once at application startup (a `lifespan` handler), not per request, and size it with the number of worker processes in mind.

questions.prompt: Match each Alembic term with its meaning.

right.text: The table that stores the current revision id
The revision a migration file builds on, forming a chain
Applies every pending revision up to the newest
Reverts the most recently applied revision
A migration operation that emits `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN`
The command that drops the whole database
The setting that auto-creates tables on import

questions.explanation: Alembic keeps one row (the current revision) in `alembic_version`, unlike tools that record every applied script. Revisions form a linked list through `down_revision`, and branches need an explicit merge.

questions.prompt: Write the two shell commands that generate an Alembic revision named `"add status"` by comparing the models with the database, and then apply all pending revisions.

checks.label: gives the revision a message with -m
applies migrations with alembic upgrade head

questions.model:
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add status"
alembic upgrade head
questions.explanation: Always read the generated script: autogenerate cannot detect column renames (it emits drop + add), many constraint changes or data migrations. `alembic downgrade -1` steps back one revision.

questions.prompt: Write the body of an Alembic `upgrade()` function that adds a nullable `status` column of type `String(20)` to the table `orders`, using `op` and `sqlalchemy` imported as `sa`.
questions.explanation: Verified against a real table. Adding a nullable column is the safe first step of an expand/contract change; backfill in batches and add `NOT NULL` in a later release. Write the matching `downgrade()` with `op.drop_column`.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: `alembic revision --autogenerate` detects a renamed column and emits an `ALTER ... RENAME COLUMN`.
questions.reason: Autogenerate compares column names between the models and the database, so a renamed column looks like one dropped and one added column.

whys.d: Correct: R is true and explains why A is false; the generated script would drop the old column (and its data) and add a new one, so you must edit it into op.alter_column(..., new_column_name=...).

questions.explanation: Always read the generated script. Autogenerate also misses many constraint changes and any data migration.

questions.prompt: Select all practices that make an Alembic-managed schema change safer for a zero-downtime PostgreSQL deployment.

options.text: Add the new column as nullable, backfill in batches, then add `NOT NULL` in a later revision.
options.why: Avoids long locks and works with old and new code.

options.text: Rename a column in one revision while old and new code are both running.
options.why: The old version breaks the moment its column disappears.
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside a transaction block.

options.text: Call `alembic upgrade head` in every worker's `lifespan` handler at startup.
options.why: Many workers racing to migrate invites lock contention and half-applied changes.

options.text: Run `alembic upgrade head` once as a deploy step before the new application version starts.
options.why: A single migration run avoids races between workers.

questions.explanation: Think in two phases per breaking change: expand (additive, compatible), then contract (cleanup after every instance uses the new shape).

questions.prompt: Where should a FastAPI application create its SQLAlchemy engine?

options.text: Inside each request handler, so that every single request gets a fresh pool of its own.
options.why: A new engine per request defeats pooling and opens a new connection each time.

options.text: Once per process, at startup or module level, shared by all requests.
options.why: Correct: the engine owns the connection pool, which only helps if it is reused.

options.text: Inside each dependency call, then disposed when the request ends.
options.why: Creating and disposing pools per request wastes time and connections.

options.text: In a background task that rebuilds it every minute.
options.why: There is no reason to rebuild a healthy engine; `pool_pre_ping` handles dead connections.

questions.explanation: Sessions are cheap and per request; the engine and its pool are long-lived and per process.
